what_its_for: Doxorubicin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including breast cancer, bladder cancer, lung cancer, stomach cancer, ovarian cancer, thyroid cancer, and certain leukemias and lymphomas. It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection or infusion (drip) directly into your vein (IV) by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic. You will NEVER give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion session may take anywhere from a few minutes to several hours depending on your specific treatment plan. Make sure to tell your nurse right away if you feel any burning, stinging, or pain near the IV site during the infusion, as this medicine can cause serious skin damage if it leaks outside the vein.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body size (height and weight), the type of cancer being treated, and your overall health. Doxorubicin is usually given in cycles — for example, once every 3 to 4 weeks — to give your body time to recover between treatments. There is also a lifetime maximum total dose limit for this medicine to protect your heart, so your doctor will track how much you have received over your entire treatment history. Never try to adjust your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because doxorubicin is given by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting, missing a scheduled appointment should be handled by contacting your cancer care team right away. Do not skip or delay your infusion without first talking to your doctor or nurse. They will reschedule your treatment as quickly as safely possible and adjust your plan if needed.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home — it is prepared and stored by pharmacy staff at the hospital or infusion center under special conditions. If for any reason you are given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, keep them safely locked away out of reach of children and pets, and follow all instructions provided by your pharmacist or nurse.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your immune system and makes it easier for you to get seriously ill. Avoid live vaccines (such as the live flu spray or shingles vaccine) during treatment — ask your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen, and blood thinners unless approved by your doctor, as they can increase bleeding risk. Avoid alcohol, as it can make side effects worse and affect your liver. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child during treatment, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby — use effective birth control. Do not breastfeed while on this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this is a medical emergency during chemotherapy), unusual bleeding or bruising, chest pain, shortness of breath, or irregular heartbeat, severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control, mouth sores that are so painful you cannot eat or drink, redness, swelling, blistering, or peeling of skin especially on hands and feet (hand-foot syndrome), signs of infection such as chills, sweating, or feeling very unwell, yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), or swelling in your legs or sudden weight gain. Also note that your urine may turn red or orange for 1 to 2 days after your infusion — this is normal and not a reason to worry, but call your doctor if you are unsure.
when_it_works: Some people begin to see results within the first few cycles of treatment, but it often takes several weeks to months of treatment before your doctor can fully measure how well the medicine is working. Your doctor will order regular tests, scans, and blood work to check your progress. It is important to complete your full treatment plan even if you feel well or do not notice immediate changes.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): You may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart problems and infections. Your doctor will monitor you very closely. Pregnant women: Do NOT use this medicine during pregnancy. It can seriously harm or cause birth defects in an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you think you may be pregnant. Women who could become pregnant and men: Use reliable birth control during treatment and for several months after your last dose. Ask your doctor how long you need to continue birth control. Breastfeeding mothers: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for a period of time after your last dose — ask your doctor for specific guidance. People with heart problems: Doxorubicin can weaken the heart over time. Your doctor will check your heart function with tests (like an echocardiogram) before and during treatment. Tell your doctor about any existing heart conditions. People with liver problems: Your dose may need to be lowered because this medicine is processed by the liver. Your liver function will be checked regularly.
